title: Canyon Run
description: Canyon Run is an Expo React Native app for GPS route capture, map visualization, and elevation-aware run review.
overview: A mobile canyon tracking companion that records location points by time or distance interval, stores runs in JSON, and lets users inspect route and elevation behavior after each session.
highlights: GPS interval-based point capture
Route + elevation visualization
Portable JSON import/export
demoTitle: Route tracking flow and map inspection
demoDescription: Canyon Run focuses on practical run telemetry: capture points in real time, persist sessions safely, and explore map/elevation details after recording.
demoBullets: Location permission + watch subscription
Point simplification for map performance
Saved run browsing with per-route details

diagramSteps.title: Capture
diagramSteps.detail: Location updates are sampled and converted into route points with timestamps and altitude.

diagramSteps.title: Persist
diagramSteps.detail: Runs are normalized and written to JSON so sessions are portable and recoverable.

diagramSteps.title: Inspect
diagramSteps.detail: Saved sessions can be reviewed on map and elevation views for route analysis.

systemDesign: Canyon Run splits capture, storage, and visualization responsibilities into separate modules. That separation makes it easier to evolve map UX without risking GPS capture reliability or data persistence behavior.
learned: This project reinforced mobile sensor-system design tradeoffs: collect enough points for useful maps, but aggressively guard performance and persistence so sessions are never lost.

title: Insert
description: Recipe app built with React Native, MongoDB, and AWS.
overview: A cross-platform recipe experience with cloud-backed data storage and a mobile-first interface for browsing and saving meals.
highlights: Cloud database support
Recipe browsing
Mobile-first UI
demoDescription: The layout is designed around quick browsing, recipe previews, and straightforward save actions so users can move fast in the kitchen.
demoBullets: Recipe list and detail views
MongoDB-backed content
AWS deployment path

diagramSteps.title: Request
diagramSteps.detail: The mobile app requests recipe data from the backend.

diagramSteps.title: Store
diagramSteps.detail: MongoDB keeps the recipe content and user data organized.

diagramSteps.title: Deliver
diagramSteps.detail: AWS hosts the app and makes the experience accessible across devices.

systemDesign: The system separates the mobile UI from the persistent data layer, which keeps the app easier to scale and simpler to maintain. MongoDB provides flexible content storage while AWS handles deployment and availability.
learned: I learned how to combine mobile UX with a cloud-backed architecture so the product can grow beyond a local prototype.

title: ESP32 Tamagotchi Clone
description: ESP32-based Tamagotchi clone featuring SSD1306 OLED display, three GPIO buttons, and active buzzer interaction.
overview: A playful embedded project that combines hardware buttons, display output, and sound feedback to recreate the classic virtual pet experience.
highlights: OLED display output
Button input handling
Active buzzer feedback
demoTitle: A tiny pet with real hardware feedback
demoDescription: The display, buttons, and buzzer work together to give the user visible and audible feedback as the virtual pet changes state.
demoBullets: SSD1306 OLED screen
Three-button controls
Active buzzer responses

diagramSteps.title: Input
diagramSteps.detail: GPIO buttons capture the player’s actions.

diagramSteps.title: Process
diagramSteps.detail: The ESP32 updates the pet’s state and logic.

diagramSteps.title: Output
diagramSteps.detail: The OLED and buzzer provide visible and audible feedback.

systemDesign: The project uses a simple embedded event loop: capture button input, update the virtual pet state, and reflect that state on the OLED with sound cues. That keeps the logic predictable and easy to debug on hardware.
learned: I learned how hardware constraints shape software design, especially when you need fast, understandable feedback from a very small interface.

title: OrderInventory
description: Company-scoped inventory app that imports Excel workbooks, routes edits through admin approval, and keeps versioned audit history.
overview: OrderInventory is one Expo Router codebase targeting Android, iOS and web. Members import messy Excel sheets, which are normalized client-side, then published or submitted for admin approval through Firebase Cloud Functions backed by Firestore with security rules.
highlights: Excel parser maps arbitrary headers to canonical fields using an alias table with exact match first, then substring fuzzy match
Unmapped columns are preserved as customFields so no spreadsheet data is lost
Join codes are 12 chars from an unambiguous alphabet via crypto.randomBytes, stored only as SHA-256 hashes, and expire after 60 seconds
All writes go through callable Cloud Functions with company-admin checks, plus Firestore rules, audit logging and immutable inventory snapshots
demoDescription: The core workflow turns an arbitrary spreadsheet into validated inventory rows and moves them through an approval pipeline.
demoBullets: Upload an .xlsx file and see headers auto-mapped to item code, name, quantity, unit, location and status
Members submit changes for approval while admins review and approve or reject
Admins generate short-lived join codes to add teammates to a company
Browse earlier inventory snapshots and export the current inventory back to Excel
codeTitle: Fuzzy header matching for Excel import

diagramSteps.title: Parse
diagramSteps.detail: SheetJS reads the first worksheet, finds the header row, maps columns by alias and coerces quantity to a number.

diagramSteps.title: Authenticate
diagramSteps.detail: The client refreshes its Firebase ID token before every callable Function request.

diagramSteps.title: Authorize
diagramSteps.detail: Cloud Functions verify company membership or admin role, then write inventory, snapshots and audit entries with the Admin SDK.

diagramSteps.title: Review
diagramSteps.detail: Member submissions wait as pending approvals until an admin approves or rejects them.

systemDesign: A thin Expo client does Excel parsing locally and calls callable Cloud Functions for every protected read and write. Functions use the Admin SDK, check company roles, write audit records and versioned snapshots to Firestore, and a scheduled function deletes expired join-code hashes. Firestore security rules add a second authorization layer.
learned: I learned to keep trust on the server: the client only parses and displays, while Cloud Functions and Firestore rules decide what is allowed. Building the header matcher taught me how forgiving spreadsheet import has to be, and that fuzzy matching needs an exact-match pass first to avoid wrong mappings. Hashing short-lived join codes was my first practical use of storing only a digest of a secret.

title: Sproutie
description: Plant care app with an Express and MongoDB backend that wraps the Trefle plant API and stores each user's plant collection.
overview: Sproutie is a React Native/Expo plant-care app paired with a Node.js/Express server. Users authenticate with Firebase, search plant species through the server, and save plants to a personal collection with growth stages, notes and care reminders. Weather-based watering notifications are described in the README as a goal.
highlights: Duplicate-save guard looks up the compound key (firebaseUid, trefleId) and returns HTTP 409 instead of inserting twice
Mongoose compound indexes, including a unique (firebaseUid, trefleId) index on favorites, keep per-user lookups fast
TrefleAPI service class wraps the third-party API, appends the token correctly with ? or &, and URL-encodes search queries
Schema models care reminders (type, frequency, lastDone, nextDue) and growth stages per plant
demoDescription: The server exposes REST endpoints that the app uses to find plants and manage a personal collection.
demoBullets: Search species with GET /api/plants/search?q=
Save a plant to a user's collection with POST /api/plants/save
List a user's plants newest first and remove entries by id
Create the Mongo user record right after Firebase registration

diagramSteps.title: Authenticate
diagramSteps.detail: Firebase handles sign-in; the app posts the Firebase UID and email to /api/users to create the Mongo profile.

diagramSteps.title: Search
diagramSteps.detail: The app calls the server, which proxies Trefle with the API token kept in an environment variable.

diagramSteps.title: Validate
diagramSteps.detail: The save route checks required fields and rejects duplicates by (firebaseUid, trefleId).

diagramSteps.title: Persist
diagramSteps.detail: A UserPlant document is created with Trefle data plus user fields such as notes, photos and care reminders.

systemDesign: A React Native client talks to an Express REST API split into routes, models and a service layer. Mongoose models hold users, saved plants, favorites and search history with compound indexes on the Firebase UID. The server hides the Trefle API token from the client. Note that the user id is taken from the request body, so server-side token verification is not yet implemented.
learned: I learned to separate routes, models and an external-API service class, and to use compound indexes and 409 responses to keep saves idempotent. Reading my own code back, I also see that trusting a userId from the request body is a gap; the next step is verifying Firebase ID tokens on the server.

title: Spotify Friend
description: React Native prototype exploring Spotify's PKCE authorization flow, with a planned song play-count tracker.
overview: The repo contains an Expo React Native App.js with TODOs for tallying song plays in a dictionary, and an assets/script.js that implements pieces of the Spotify Authorization Code with PKCE flow: verifier generation, SHA-256 challenge, token exchange and profile fetch. It is unfinished and not wired together.
highlights: PKCE code verifier built from 128 random characters
S256 code challenge using SHA-256 and base64url encoding (replace + and /, strip =)
Token exchange posts authorization code plus verifier to the Spotify token endpoint
Planned song-count dictionary; the auth flow is incomplete and the app does not run end to end
demoDescription: A prototype of the Spotify login steps; the UI is not finished.
demoBullets: Generates verifier and challenge for PKCE
Exchanges code for an access token
Fetches the profile from /v1/me
Song play counting is still TODO

diagramSteps.title: Verifier
diagramSteps.detail: Generate a random 128 character string and keep it in local storage.

diagramSteps.title: Challenge
diagramSteps.detail: SHA-256 hash the verifier and base64url encode it.

diagramSteps.title: Authorize
diagramSteps.detail: Redirect to Spotify with the S256 challenge (the redirect line is commented out).

diagramSteps.title: Token
diagramSteps.detail: Exchange the returned code and verifier for an access token, then call /v1/me.

systemDesign: A React Native App.js shell plus a script module holding the OAuth helper functions. The pieces are not yet connected, and the script mixes Node-style crypto with a mobile client, which I would need to fix.
learned: I learned how PKCE protects the authorization code flow without a client secret. The code also shows my limits: it uses Math.random for the verifier and Node modules in a mobile app, so I would switch to a secure random source and an Expo-compatible crypto library next.

title: Dino Game
description: A Chrome-style endless runner built with vanilla JavaScript and the HTML5 Canvas.
overview: A single-page canvas game where a dinosaur jumps over randomly spawned cacti. It uses a requestAnimationFrame loop, simple gravity physics, and AABB collision detection, all in one small script with no libraries.
highlights: requestAnimationFrame game loop that clears and redraws the canvas every frame
Gravity physics: velocityY += gravity each frame, with the dino clamped to the ground using Math.min
Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) collision detection between the dino and each cactus
Weighted random cactus spawning (about 70% small, 20% medium, 10% large) on a 1 second interval, capped at 5 live obstacles
demoDescription: Run the game in a browser and jump over cacti until you collide with one.
demoBullets: Press Space or Arrow Up to jump
Jumping is only allowed while the dino is on the ground
Score increases every frame
On collision the sprite swaps to a dead dino and the loop stops

diagramSteps.title: Input
diagramSteps.detail: A keydown listener sets velocityY to -10 when the dino is on the ground.

diagramSteps.title: Update
diagramSteps.detail: Gravity is added to velocityY, dino.y is clamped at ground level, and cacti move left by velocityX.

diagramSteps.title: Collide
diagramSteps.detail: Each cactus is checked against the dino with an AABB overlap test.

diagramSteps.title: Render
diagramSteps.detail: The canvas is cleared and sprites plus the score are redrawn, then the next frame is requested.

systemDesign: Everything lives in one script with module-level state (dino and cactus objects, velocity, gravity, score, gameOver). A requestAnimationFrame loop drives updates and rendering, while a separate setInterval spawns obstacles. Spawned cacti are copied from a template object and stored in a small array that drops the oldest entry past five.
learned: I learned how a basic game loop works: update state, test collisions, then redraw. I got comfortable with simple gravity physics and AABB overlap checks. Looking back, the game speed is tied to frame rate and cactus spawning uses a fixed timer, so a fixed timestep and a spawn gap tied to speed would make it more consistent.

title: React Weather
description: A React weather app that looks up a city and shows current conditions from OpenWeatherMap.
overview: Users type a city name and the app fetches current weather from the OpenWeatherMap API in imperial units, then shows an icon matching the condition plus temperature, min/max, humidity and wind. A 404 response shows a city-not-found error.
highlights: useEffect triggered by city state to fetch data from the REST API whenever a new city is submitted
Async fetch with HTTP 404 handling that clears stale data and sets an error flag
Lookup-table mapping of the API weather.main value to an icon image
Component split into Info, Card, Block, Menu and Navigation with CSS Modules styling
demoDescription: Enter a city name and submit to see its current weather.
demoBullets: Empty submissions trigger an alert asking for a city
Condition icon is chosen from the API response
Shows temperature, min, max, humidity and wind speed
Unknown cities display an error message

diagramSteps.title: Submit
diagramSteps.detail: The form handler reads the input and sets the city state.

diagramSteps.title: Fetch
diagramSteps.detail: A useEffect on city calls the OpenWeatherMap current weather endpoint.

diagramSteps.title: Handle
diagramSteps.detail: A 404 sets the error state; otherwise the JSON is stored in weatherData.

diagramSteps.title: Render
diagramSteps.detail: The matching icon and weather values are rendered from state.

systemDesign: A Create React App client with no backend. The Info component owns three pieces of state (city, error, weatherData) and calls the public API directly from the browser. Weather icons are imported as a module and mapped by condition name. Styling uses CSS Modules.
learned: I learned the useState and useEffect data-fetching pattern and how to handle an error response from an API. Honestly, the API key is hardcoded in the client source, which I would now move to an environment variable or a proxy. The weathers array check also does nothing useful, and a network failure other than 404 is not handled.

title: geoToDo
description: A full-stack task manager with an Expo React Native client and an Express/MongoDB API, aimed at location-aware to-dos.
overview: The mobile app shows tasks in Today, Future and Locations tabs and lets tasks move between Open, WIP and Closed. The Node/Express server connects to MongoDB and serves task data over a REST API. The geolocation features are planned in the structure, but I did not find actual distance or geofence code in the files I read.
highlights: Two-part architecture: Expo Router app in toDo/ and Express API in server/
Controller-per-resource API layout (runs, tasks, users, locations) using Express routers
MongoDB access through the official driver with Stable API strict mode and env-based URI
Tabbed task views (Today, Future, Locations) with status filtering and PATCH-based status updates described in the README
demoDescription: Start the Express server with a MongoDB URI, then launch the Expo app.
demoBullets: Server needs MONGO_URI in a .env file
GET /api/runs returns documents from MongoDB
Expo app renders User and ToDo components from the index route
Client expects the server at localhost:3000

diagramSteps.title: App
diagramSteps.detail: Expo Router renders the User and ToDo components.

diagramSteps.title: Request
diagramSteps.detail: The client uses fetch against the Express API.

diagramSteps.title: API
diagramSteps.detail: Express routes call the MongoDB driver and return JSON.

diagramSteps.title: Store
diagramSteps.detail: Task documents live in a MongoDB collection.

systemDesign: A separate client and server. The client uses file-based routing (Expo Router) with tab components per view. The server loads the MongoDB URI from the environment, enables CORS and JSON parsing, and organizes endpoints into controller files per resource. Currently only the runs route is clearly wired up in server.js.
learned: I learned how to connect an Expo client to an Express and MongoDB backend and keep secrets in environment variables. Honestly, the server opens and closes a MongoDB connection on every request, which is wasteful; a shared connection would be better. The location features are not implemented in the code I reviewed, so this is more of a CRUD foundation so far.

title: Schedule Short
description: An Expo app that imports a staff schedule CSV and parses it into per-person schedule objects.
overview: Users pick a CSV file with expo-document-picker. A custom parser walks the file line by line, detects the day-label row, the date row and role section headers (RN, CST, FA), and builds a Person object for each employee with their dated availability.
highlights: Hand-written CSV parser that identifies header, date and role-section rows by column content and a regex (d{1,2}-Mon)
Person class that stores a schedule keyed by date, with a date-to-weekday map
Role tracking: the current section (RN, CST, FA) is remembered and applied to each person row below it
getWeek(n) slices the date-keyed schedule into 7-day windows and throws on out-of-range weeks
demoDescription: Choose a CSV schedule file and the app parses it into structured people and dates.
demoBullets: Only CSV files are accepted
A Working indicator shows during processing
Parsed people and counts are logged to the console
Runs on web, iOS and Android through Expo

diagramSteps.title: Pick
diagramSteps.detail: expo-document-picker returns a CSV file that is validated by type.

diagramSteps.title: Scan
diagramSteps.detail: Each line is split on commas and checked for day-label, date and role rows.

diagramSteps.title: Build
diagramSteps.detail: Name rows create or update Person objects with D, X or B values by date.

diagramSteps.title: Query
diagramSteps.detail: Methods like checkDate and getWeek read the result.

systemDesign: The Expo app has a screen that calls a file-import component and then a pure parsing function in controller/organize.js, which returns an object of Person instances keyed by name. A small Express server folder also exists. The day.js and week.js controller files are empty placeholders.
learned: I learned to parse a messy, real-world spreadsheet export by detecting row types instead of assuming a clean format, and to model the result with a class. The parser is fragile: it splits on commas, so quoted fields would break it, and it relies on fixed column positions. The Person.changeRole method also references a field that does not exist, so I would clean that up and add tests.

title: Authentication
description: Express and MongoDB authentication API with bcrypt password hashing and JWT token issuing, paired with a React client.
overview: A learning project that builds a username/password auth backend. The Express server mounts a router at /api/auth with register and login endpoints, stores users in MongoDB through a Mongoose schema, hashes passwords with bcrypt, and signs JSON Web Tokens with a secret from environment variables.
highlights: Registration salts and hashes passwords with bcrypt.genSalt(10) and bcrypt.hash before saving
Login returns a signed JWT built from the user id, with the secret read from process.env
Separate jwtHelper utility with generateToken (1 hour expiry) and verifyToken that returns null on failure
Mongoose schema enforces required, unique and trimmed usernames and has a verifyPassword method using bcrypt.compare
Generic 'Invalid username or password' message so login does not reveal which part was wrong
demoDescription: Register a user, then log in to receive a token the client can attach to later requests.
demoBullets: POST /api/auth/register creates a user with a hashed password
Duplicate usernames are rejected with a 400
POST /api/auth/login checks the password and returns a JWT
Configuration such as MONGODB_URI and JWT_SECRET comes from environment variables
codeTitle: Register route with salted bcrypt hashing

diagramSteps.title: Client request
diagramSteps.detail: React client posts username and password as JSON to /api/auth.

diagramSteps.title: Lookup
diagramSteps.detail: Mongoose queries the User collection by username.

diagramSteps.title: Hash or compare
diagramSteps.detail: Register hashes with a bcrypt salt; login compares against the stored hash.

diagramSteps.title: Token
diagramSteps.detail: On successful login the server signs a JWT and returns it.

systemDesign: A three-folder repo (client, front, server). The server is an Express app with CORS and JSON middleware, a mounted auth router, a Mongoose User model, and a small JWT helper module. Secrets and the database URI are read from environment variables.
learned: I learned the basic shape of a token-based auth backend: salting and hashing passwords, never storing plaintext, and signing JWTs with an env secret. The code is still a work in progress. The login route calls bcrypt.password instead of bcrypt.compare, signs its token without an expiry (the helper has a 1 hour one but the route does not use it), and jwtHelper mixes ES imports with module.exports. Writing it showed me how easy those mistakes are, and that I need tests and a verify-token middleware to protect routes.

title: Login Page
description: React and Express registration and login app backed by MySQL, with bcrypt password hashing and an email existence check.
overview: A full-stack authentication demo. The Express server connects to a local MySQL database, creates the database and a user table if they are missing, and exposes routes for adding, reading, updating and deleting users plus a login route that compares a submitted password against a stored bcrypt hash. The React client provides the registration and login forms with validation.
highlights: Passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds) before insertion into MySQL
Server bootstraps itself: falls back to creating the testServer database and a user table with a UNIQUE email column
Login route fetches the user by email and uses bcrypt.compare on the stored hash
/checkEmail endpoint returns { exists } so the client can validate an email before registering
README describes password validation and email checking on the React side
demoDescription: Sign up with an email and password, then log in against the MySQL-backed server.
demoBullets: Registration form validates the password and checks whether the email already exists
New passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes
Login responds with success, incorrect password, or not found
Requires a local MySQL server and the Express server running

diagramSteps.title: React form
diagramSteps.detail: Validates input and calls the Express API with the email and password.

diagramSteps.title: Express route
diagramSteps.detail: CORS and body-parser middleware parse the JSON request.

diagramSteps.title: MySQL query
diagramSteps.detail: The user row is looked up or inserted in the user table.

diagramSteps.title: bcrypt
diagramSteps.detail: Passwords are hashed on write and compared on login.

systemDesign: A two-folder monolith: a client React app and a single server.js Express file. The server owns a single MySQL connection and creates its schema on startup. Everything is on localhost with hard-coded connection settings.
learned: I learned how a full-stack login fits together and how bcrypt hashing works with a SQL database. Honestly, the server is a learning prototype: many routes are GET requests that mutate data, and queries are built by string interpolation, which is open to SQL injection. Login also returns plain text and no session or token. If I revisit it I would use parameterized queries, POST/DELETE verbs, and issue a token or session.

title: ToDo (React Native Task Tracker)
description: An Expo / React Native to-do app with status counters and tasks persisted on-device with AsyncStorage.
overview: ToDo is a React Native app built with Expo. Tasks are instances of a small Task class (text, date, type, tags, description) held in React state and serialized to AsyncStorage as JSON. A header row shows live counters for Complete, ToDo, Progress and Wait. A simpler sibling repo, ToDoIOS, is a minimal version of the same idea that keeps tasks in memory and tracks completion in a map keyed by task text.
highlights: Persists the task list as JSON in AsyncStorage and rehydrates it into Task objects on startup
Status counters (Complete, ToDo, Progress, Wait) built from an object map and memoized with useMemo
Add flow with input validation and a collapsible menu component
ToDoIOS variant: FlatList rendering, tap-to-strike-through, and a two-press confirm for Remove All
demoDescription: Add a task, see the counters update, and reopen the app to confirm tasks are still there.
demoBullets: Tap Add Task to open the input menu
Empty input is rejected with an alert
Tasks are saved to AsyncStorage after each add
Status chips show a count per category

diagramSteps.title: Input
diagramSteps.detail: User types a task and description in the Menu component; empty input is rejected.

diagramSteps.title: State
diagramSteps.detail: A new Task object is appended to the tasks array held in useState.

diagramSteps.title: Persist
diagramSteps.detail: The array is stringified and written to AsyncStorage under the 'tasks' key.

diagramSteps.title: Rehydrate
diagramSteps.detail: On mount, useEffect reads the key and rebuilds Task instances, restoring Date objects.

systemDesign: A single screen component owns all state and passes setters down to child components (Menu, TaskBox). Storage is the only persistence layer, with no backend. Because JSON drops class methods and Dates become strings, loading re-wraps each record in the Task class.
learned: I learned that JSON serialization loses class methods and turns Dates into strings, so I had to rebuild Task instances when loading from AsyncStorage. I also learned the code works but has rough edges: the component holds many state variables and logs a lot, and my ToDoIOS version keys completion by task text, which breaks with duplicate tasks. Next time I would use ids.

title: toDoGeo (Task Countdown App)
description: An Expo Router TypeScript client with a task model that computes a live time-remaining countdown, plus a stub server folder.
overview: toDoGeo is an early-stage Expo Router app with a client and server folder. The working part is the ToDo component and a Task class that stores title, description, due date and completion, and computes a days/hours/minutes/seconds string from the due date. A one-second interval re-renders the list, and the remaining time is color-styled by urgency. The Locations component is only a stub, so no geofencing or distance math exists in the code yet.
highlights: Task class computes a days/hr/min/sec countdown with floor and modulo math on millisecond differences
setInterval tick re-renders the list every second, with cleanup on unmount
Urgency styling: more than 3 days, more than 1 day, or less than 1 day
Includes a Jest test file for the Task class
demoDescription: Seeded tasks show live ticking countdowns that change color as the due date approaches.
demoBullets: Toggle a task complete with a Switch
Clear completed removes finished tasks
Countdown updates every second
Color changes at 3-day and 1-day thresholds

diagramSteps.title: Model
diagramSteps.detail: Task holds title, description, due Date and completed flag.

diagramSteps.title: Tick
diagramSteps.detail: useEffect sets a 1s interval that copies the task array to force a re-render.

diagramSteps.title: Compute
diagramSteps.detail: Each render subtracts Date.now() from the due date and formats the parts.

diagramSteps.title: Style
diagramSteps.detail: A threshold function picks a high, medium or low urgency style.

systemDesign: The app uses file-based routing; the index screen composes User and ToDo components. Tasks are hardcoded sample data in component state, with no persistence or networking yet. The server folder only contains a package.json, and the Locations component is a placeholder for the intended location feature.
learned: I learned how to turn a millisecond difference into days, hours, minutes and seconds with floor and modulo, and how to run a timer safely in a React effect. Being honest about the state of the repo: the location-based part is not implemented yet, the data is hardcoded, and the Clear completed handler mutates state directly, which I left as a TODO to refactor.

title: my-life (Notes App with Express + MySQL API)
description: A React web app scaffold paired with an Express and MySQL REST API for storing notes.
overview: my-life is a Create React App front end (App, Main and Nav components) with a Node/Express server that connects to a local MySQL database, creates the 'notes' database and table if missing, and exposes endpoints to add, fetch, list and delete notes. It is an early prototype: the sibling repos noteDiary and CalenderDiary are near-empty scaffolds, so they are not documented separately.
highlights: Express REST API with add, get, delete and list-all note routes
Self-bootstrapping schema: creates the database and notes table if absent
Table uses auto-increment id and a default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP date_created column
Insert uses mysql's parameterized SET ? form
demoDescription: Run the server on port 4000 and call the note endpoints from the React client or any HTTP tool.
demoBullets: POST /addnote with note and subject
GET /getallnotes returns all rows as JSON
DELETE /deletenote/:id removes a note
Requires a local MySQL server

diagramSteps.title: Client
diagramSteps.detail: The React app sends JSON to the Express server.

diagramSteps.title: Middleware
diagramSteps.detail: cors and body-parser allow cross-origin calls and parse JSON bodies.

diagramSteps.title: Route
diagramSteps.detail: A route builds a SQL statement for create, read or delete.

diagramSteps.title: MySQL
diagramSteps.detail: The notes table stores id, note text, subject and creation timestamp.

systemDesign: A two-tier setup: a CRA front end and a single-file Express server on port 4000 using callback-style mysql queries. The schema is created at startup, so no migration step is needed locally. The database connects as root with an empty password, which is only suitable for local development.
learned: I learned how to wire an Express server to MySQL and bootstrap a schema at startup. Looking back honestly, the code has flaws: the get and delete routes build SQL by string interpolation, which is open to SQL injection, errors are only logged so the response can still crash, and getnote does not return the row. I would use parameterized queries and proper error handling next time.

title: Fitness Site
description: A multi-page fitness website built with plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, featuring muscle group pages, a video carousel, dark mode and form validation.
overview: Fitness Site is a static front-end project with no framework or build step. It has a main fitness.html page, a catalog page, per-muscle-group pages, and a single script.js that handles section switching, a vertical video carousel, a dark mode toggle and contact form validation.
highlights: Class-based section switching with a toggleDisplay helper that hides the current section and shows the next
Vertical video carousel that rotates items by moving DOM nodes with insertBefore and appendChild
Dark mode implemented by toggling a single dark-mode class on the body from a checkbox
Contact form validation with required-field checks and a regular expression for email format

systemDesign: A static multi-page site served directly from files. Layout and theme live in CSS (styles.css, catalog_style.css), behavior lives in one script.js, and muscle group content is split into separate pages under the musclegroups folder. State is kept in the DOM and one global variable, with no backend.
learned: This project taught me how far plain DOM APIs can go without a framework. Looking back, the navigation code has rough edges: currentClass starts as an HTMLCollection rather than a string, and the carousel registers two click handlers on the up button that overlap. I would clean those up, and a component framework would make the state handling simpler.

title: React Spotify Playlist App (Work in Progress)
description: An in-progress React playlist builder with a client split into SearchBar, SearchResults, Playlist, Tracklist and Track components, plus an Express and MySQL server scaffold.
overview: This repo has a client/server layout. The React client defines a component tree for searching tracks and building a playlist, with App holding the state. The Spotify API module and several App handlers are still stubs, and the Express server currently only sets up middleware and a MySQL connection.
highlights: Component tree split by responsibility: App, SearchBar, SearchResults, Playlist, Tracklist and Track
App owns search results, playlist name and playlist tracks in useState and passes handlers down
Handlers wrapped in useCallback, with addTracks skipping tracks already in the playlist by id
Express server scaffold with cors, body-parser and a MySQL connection, with bcrypt required for later auth work
demoDescription: The intended flow is to search for tracks, add them to a named playlist and save it. The README describes this flow, but the Spotify API connection and several handlers are not implemented yet.
demoBullets: Search term is passed from SearchBar up to App
Results render through SearchResults and Tracklist
Add button appends a track unless its id is already present
Remove, rename and save handlers are stubbed

diagramSteps.title: App state
diagramSteps.detail: Holds search results, playlist name and playlist tracks, and defines the handlers.

diagramSteps.title: Tracklist and Track
diagramSteps.detail: Render arrays of track objects with add or remove buttons wired to App callbacks.

diagramSteps.title: Spotify util
diagramSteps.detail: spotify.js is meant to talk to the Spotify API but currently contains only a comment.

systemDesign: A React client in client/ with CSS Modules per component, and an Express server in server/ with cors, JSON body parsing and a MySQL connection. State lives in App and flows down as props, with callbacks flowing back up. The Spotify API and OAuth integration are not implemented yet.
learned: I practiced lifting state up and structuring components around single responsibilities. The project is honestly unfinished: removeTrack, updatePlaylist and savePlaylist are empty stubs, the Spotify module has no API calls, and the server has no routes. Finishing it would mean implementing the OAuth flow and those handlers.
